etymology: Hebrew midbar Yehudah, the desert of Judah; the tribal name Yehudah comes from yadah, to praise or give thanks.
biblical_def: Southward and eastward of the hill country of Judah, falling away toward the salt sea, lies a parched and broken land of chalk and stone where little grows and less water runs. Hither the children of the Kenite went up out of the city of palm trees to dwell among the people (Jdg 1:16); hither David fled from the face of Saul and hid in its strong holds; and here, athirst in body and soul, he sang, “O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is” (Psa 63:1). The wilderness of Judah is the very emblem of the believer’s estate in this present world — a dry and thirsty land, where the flesh finds no water, and the soul is driven to seek the LORD betimes. What the land withholds, God Himself supplies; He is the portion and the fountain of them that thirst. And it was into this same waste that the forerunner came, for in those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea (Mat 3:1), crying Repent, and pointing to the Lamb. The dry land, then, is where God trains His pilgrims to thirst, to repent, and to look for the water of life that He alone can give.
webster_summary: The parched desert east and south of Judah’s hill country, sloping to the salt sea; David’s refuge, the setting of Psalm 63, and where John the Baptist preached repentance.
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF JUDAH, the dry region east and south of Judah’s hill country, toward the salt sea.

There John the Baptist preached, crying Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
A figure of the believer’s pilgrim estate, where the soul is driven to the fountain of living waters.

corruption_summary: A real desert region raises no live quarrel; the truth to recover is that the dry land is God’s appointed school of thirst and repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness of Judah is a plain geographical fact, its chalk hills and dry wadis still to be seen, and no controversy attends it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God ordains the dry place to teach His people to thirst after Him. David did not curse the desert; he sought God in it early. John did not shun it; he preached repentance from it. Let the believer learn that the barren season is not God’s absence but His schooling, driving the soul to the fountain of living waters.
roots_summary: The name Judah comes from a root meaning to praise; the wilderness that bears it teaches praise wrung from a thirsting soul.
roots_lines: Judah — Hebrew Yehudah, from yadah, to praise or give thanks.

etymology: Hebrew midbar Dammeseq, the desert toward Damascus, chief city of Aram (Syria), lying northeast of Israel.
biblical_def: When Elijah, spent and despairing under the juniper tree, had asked that he might die and had fled to Horeb, the LORD did not indulge his gloom but recommissioned him: “Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus” (1Ki 19:15). The wild waste that stretches toward Syria’s great city became the direction of the prophet’s renewed obedience, for there he was to anoint Hazael king over Syria, and Jehu over Israel, and Elisha the prophet in his own room. Two lessons rise from this desert road. First, the LORD is sovereign over the kings of the nations; He setteth up and He putteth down, anointing even a pagan Hazael to be a rod in His hand against a rebellious people. The thrones of Syria are His to dispose. Second, the cure for the fainting servant is not endless comfort but a fresh commission: the still small voice that had spoken so tenderly at the mount now sent Elijah back to work, back toward Damascus and the appointed tasks. The wilderness of Damascus thus preaches to every discouraged minister of God that self-pity is answered with service, and that the God who rules the empires will not waste the labour of His weakest prophet. He that ordaineth the end ordaineth also the road, though it lead through a wilderness toward a heathen throne.
webster_summary: The desert toward Damascus in Syria, whither the LORD sent the discouraged Elijah to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha (1Ki 19:15); a witness to God’s sovereignty over the nations and His recommissioning of His fainting servant.
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF DAMASCUS, the desert toward the Syrian city of Damascus.

There he was to anoint Hazael king of Syria, an instrument of judgment.
The still small voice answered the prophet’s despair with a fresh commission.
A witness that God rules the thrones of the heathen and restores His weary servants to labour.

corruption_paragraphs: The road toward Damascus through the wilderness is a matter of geography and history, uncontested.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. The LORD reigns over the kings of Syria and Assyria alike, anointing and removing them for His purposes, so that no earthly power stands outside His decree. And He heals His discouraged servants not by leaving them under the juniper but by sending them back to the appointed work. Elijah asked to die; God gave him a journey and a task. So let the weary saint hear, in the still small voice, not a lullaby but a commission.
roots_summary: Damascus, ancient head-city of Aram or Syria; the wilderness bearing its name marks the road of Elijah’s recommissioning.
roots_lines: Damascus — Hebrew Dammeseq, the chief city of Aram (Syria).

The fainting prophet was answered with a fresh commission, not with rest alone.

etymology: Hebrew midbar Yeruel, the desert of Jeruel (perhaps “founded of God” or “fear of God”), a waste tract in the wilderness of Judah between Tekoa and the cliff of Ziz above En-gedi.
biblical_def: When a great multitude of Moab and Ammon and mount Seir came against Jehoshaphat, the king feared, and set himself to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah. As the people stood before the LORD with their little ones, the Spirit came upon Jahaziel, who cried: “Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD… for the battle is not yours, but God’s.” On the morrow they went forth toward the wilderness of Jeruel (2Ch 20:16), and there they found their enemies already fallen one upon another, so that none escaped. And Judah’s part was to sing: they appointed singers unto the LORD, that should praise the beauty of holiness, saying, Praise the LORD, for his mercy endureth for ever; and when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushments against the foe. The wilderness of Jeruel is the field where faith learns that its warfare is the LORD’s, and that praise goes up before the victory is seen. Here is the gospel pattern: the outnumbered people, unable to save themselves, stand still and behold the salvation of God, and give Him the songs of the delivered. So the believer, hemmed in by enemies too strong for him, sets himself to seek the LORD, stands still, and sings, for the battle is not his but God’s.
webster_summary: A desert tract in Judah above En-gedi where the LORD Himself routed the Moab-Ammon coalition against Jehoshaphat while Judah’s singers praised (2Ch 20:16); a witness that the battle is the LORD’s and that faith praises before the victory.
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF JERUEL, a desert tract in Judah above En-gedi.
There Jehoshaphat met the great host of Moab, Ammon, and Seir (2Ch 20:16).
Jahaziel prophesied, The battle is not yours, but God’s.
Judah’s appointed singers praised, and the LORD set ambushments against the foe.
A witness that faith stands still, sings, and sees the salvation of the LORD.

corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness of Jeruel is a real place in the Judean desert, and the history of Jehoshaphat’s deliverance stands unshaken in the record.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the salvation of God’s people is God’s own work, not theirs. Jehoshaphat did not muster a cleverer army; he set himself to seek the LORD, proclaimed a fast, and set the singers before the host. Faith’s posture is to stand still and behold; faith’s music begins before the enemy falls. Recover this against every gospel of self-salvation: the battle is not ours, but God’s.
roots_summary: Jeruel likely means “founded of God” or “fear of God”; the desert so named became the theatre of God’s own victory.
roots_lines: Jeruel — Hebrew Yeruel, perhaps “founded of God” or “fear of God.”

etymology: Hebrew midbar Beer-sheba, the desert about Beersheba (“well of the oath” or “well of seven”), the southernmost region of Judah toward the Negev.
biblical_def: Cast out at Sarah’s word and Abraham’s heavy consent, Hagar took the bread and the bottle of water and departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba (Gen 21:14). When the water was spent she laid the child under a shrub and sat over against him, saying, Let me not see the death of the child, and she lifted up her voice and wept. But God heard the voice of the lad where he was, and the angel of God called to Hagar: What aileth thee? fear not. And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water, and gave the lad drink. This desert, on the southern edge of the promised land, is a witness to the God who seeth and heareth the cast-out. The well was there all along; the mercy was that God opened her eyes to it. Here shines the wideness of His providence, that even Ishmael, not the child of promise, is heard and preserved and made a great nation, for God is kind to the outcast and the stranger. Yet the entry teaches also the sovereignty of the covenant: the promise ran not through Ishmael but through Isaac, the child of the free woman, born after the Spirit. The wilderness of Beersheba thus holds both truths without confusion — a common goodness that spares the perishing, and a distinguishing grace that keeps the line of promise. God heareth the crying lad, and God keepeth His word to the seed.
webster_summary: The desert about Beersheba on Judah’s southern edge, where Hagar and Ishmael wandered and God opened her eyes to the well (Gen 21:14); a witness to the God who sees and hears the cast-out, while the promise runs through Isaac.

corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness of Beersheba is a real region at the edge of the Negev, and the account of Hagar stands as written.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the harmony of common grace and distinguishing grace. God is kind to Ishmael: He hears the lad, opens the well, and makes of him a nation. But the covenant runs through Isaac alone, as the apostle teaches that the son of the bondwoman was after the flesh and the son of the free woman by promise. Let none turn God’s general mercies into a denial of His electing purpose; He may hear the cast-out and still keep His word to the chosen seed.
roots_summary: Beersheba, “well of the oath” or “well of seven,” from Abraham’s covenant with Abimelech; the wilderness of that name lies on Judah’s southern rim.

etymology: Hebrew midbar En-gedi, “fountain of the kid”; the desert of crags and caves by the western shore of the salt sea.
biblical_def: By the springs of En-gedi, where fresh water leaps down cliffs above the salt and lifeless sea, lies a labyrinth of caves among the rocks of the wild goats. When Saul was returned from following the Philistines, they told him David was in the wilderness of En-gedi (1Sa 24:1), and he took three thousand chosen men and went to seek him upon the rocks. There, in the very cave where David and his men lay hid, Saul came in to cover his feet; and David’s men whispered that God had delivered his enemy into his hand. But David only cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe, and his heart smote him even for that, saying, The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD’s anointed. He would not stretch forth his hand, but committed his cause to God: The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee. Here is a lesson the flesh never learns of itself: vengeance belongeth to the LORD, and the man after God’s heart will not seize by violence what God hath promised to give in His time. In this restraint David foreshadowed a greater Son of David, who, when He was reviled, reviled not again, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously. The caves of En-gedi preach the patience of the anointed who waiteth on God.
webster_summary: The desert of caves and springs by the salt sea where David spared Saul’s life (1Sa 24:1); a witness that vengeance belongs to the LORD, and a figure of Christ who committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously.
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF EN-GEDI, the rocky desert by the springs of En-gedi on the salt sea.

A figure of Christ, who reviled not again but committed Himself to a righteous Judge.

corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness of En-gedi with its springs and caves is a real place above the salt sea, and David’s forbearance is written for our learning.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer must not avenge himself, but give place unto wrath, for the LORD hath said, Vengeance is mine, I will repay. David had the king in his hand and would not strike, because Saul was the LORD’s anointed and the throne was God’s to give. So the Christian, wronged and pursued, commits his cause to the righteous Judge, and waits, as his Master waited upon the cross.

etymology: Hebrew midbar Moab, the desert bordering Moab, the land of the children of Lot east of the salt sea and the river Arnon.
biblical_def: As Israel came up out of the great and terrible wilderness toward the promised land, their way lay along the eastern marches, and the LORD led them through the wilderness of Moab, the land of the children of Lot. Yet He laid a strict charge upon them: they passed by from their brethren the children of Esau and turned to pass by the way of the wilderness of Moab (Deu 2:8), for the LORD had said, Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle; for I will not give thee of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession. Here the pilgrim host is taught to keep the borders God hath set. The desert of Moab preaches first the providence that fixeth the bounds of the nations: the LORD had appointed Moab their inheritance for Lot’s sake, and Israel might not covet it. He determineth the times before appointed, and the bounds of men’s habitation. It preaches also the restraining mercy of God, who holdeth back the strong from wronging the weak by His mere command. And it preaches the pilgrim way, which skirteth the tents of the world without pitching in them: Israel passed through, but did not settle in Moab, for they sought a better country. So the church journeyeth among the nations, respecting the order God hath set, coveting no man’s land, pressing on toward the inheritance reserved in heaven.
webster_summary: The desert bordering Moab, the land of Lot’s children, through which Israel passed forbidden to vex them (Deu 2:8); a witness to the providence that fixes the borders of nations and the pilgrim way that skirts the world.
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF MOAB, the desert bordering Moab east of the salt sea.
Israel passed through it toward Canaan (Deu 2:8).
The LORD forbade them to distress the Moabites, children of Lot.
A witness that God fixes the borders and inheritances of the nations.
The pilgrim host skirted the tents of the world, seeking a better country.

corruption_summary: No live redefinition attends this desert; the truth to recover is that God appoints the bounds of the nations, and His pilgrims covet no land but the inheritance above.
corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness of Moab is a real region east of the salt sea, and Israel’s passage through it is plain history.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Most High divideth to the nations their inheritance and setteth the bounds of the people. God gave Ar to Lot’s sons and forbade Israel to seize it; He governeth the map of the world by His decree, not by the covetousness of the strong. And His people, though they must pass among the nations, are strangers and pilgrims who seek no continuing city here, but one to come.
roots_summary: Moab, the son of Lot by his elder daughter, and the nation and land descended from him; the desert on its border bears the name.

The wilderness of Moab teaches the pilgrim to keep God’s appointed bounds.

etymology: Hebrew midbar Edom, the desert of Edom (“red”), the arid land of Esau’s posterity south of the salt sea.
biblical_def: When Jehoram of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah, and the king of Edom marched by the way of the wilderness of Edom to chastise rebel Moab (2Ki 3:8), they fetched a compass of seven days’ journey, and there was no water for the host nor for the cattle that followed them. The three kings were brought to the end of themselves, and Jehoshaphat sought a prophet of the LORD, and Elisha was found. Then came the word of promise: Make this valley full of ditches; for thus saith the LORD, Ye shall not see wind, neither shall ye see rain; yet that valley shall be filled with water. And in the morning the water came by the way of Edom, and the country was filled with water, though no cloud had risen and no wind had blown. The wilderness of Edom is a standing witness that the LORD supplieth in the dry place by means unseen. He is not bound to the ordinary channels of nature; He can fill the trenches without wind or rain, from a source over the horizon, that His people may know the supply is His and not the sky’s. So He giveth grace beyond nature’s expectation, water where the heavens promised none. But the promise met a condition: dig the ditches. Faith prepareth the empty vessels; God filleth them. The dry desert of Edom bids the believer make room for a mercy he cannot see coming, and wait for the LORD to fill it.
webster_summary: The arid desert of Edom south of the salt sea, where the three kings’ army fainted for water and Elisha promised the LORD would fill the trenches without wind or rain (2Ki 3:8); a witness that God supplies by means unseen.
webster_full: WILDERNESS OF EDOM, the dry desert of Esau’s land south of the salt sea.
The three kings marched through it against Moab and found no water (2Ki 3:8).
Elisha promised the valley should be filled without wind or rain.
The water came by the way of Edom, from a source unseen.
A witness that the LORD supplies beyond nature when His people dig the ditches.

corruption_summary: No live redefinition attends this desert; the truth to recover is that the LORD supplies His people by means unseen, and faith must prepare the empty vessels He will fill.
corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness of Edom is a real region south of the salt sea, and the miracle of the filled trenches is written as history.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not confined to the ordinary means. He filled the valley without wind or rain, from waters that rose beyond the sight of the fainting army, that all might know the supply was His alone. Yet He gave the water where the ditches were dug. Grace outruns nature, but faith maketh room for it; the believer prepareth the vessel and waiteth on the LORD to fill it.

etymology: Hebrew arabah, “plain, desert, dry place”; the great rift-valley of the Jordan running from the sea of Chinnereth down to the salt sea; the KJV renders it “the plain” and “the champaign.”
biblical_def: The Arabah is the great cleft in the earth through which the Jordan runs, the deepest depression on the face of the ground, sinking from the waters of Chinnereth down to the salt sea, the lowest dry land under heaven. The KJV nameth it the plain and the champaign: Moses spake unto all Israel on this side Jordan in the wilderness, in the plain over against the Red sea (Deu 1:1), and the plain, from Chinnereth even unto the sea of the plain, even the salt sea, was reckoned to Israel (Deu 3:17). Through this low place the pilgrim people passed toward the promise, and its very depth is a parable. The way to Canaan led downward before it led up; the road to the inheritance ran through the deepest valley of all. So the Christian’s path to glory descendeth through humbling and death before it riseth. And at the bottom of the Arabah lieth the salt sea, that dead and bitter water covering the plain where Sodom stood, a standing witness to the judgment of God upon sin. The pilgrim walketh beside it and remembereth: here fire came down from heaven; here the cities of the plain became an ensample, set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire. The Arabah thus holdeth both the low road of the humble and the memorial of wrath, and bids the traveller press through the valley toward the city that hath foundations.
webster_summary: The great rift-valley of the Jordan, the lowest dry land on earth, running down to the salt sea; KJV “the plain,” “the champaign” (Deu 1:1; 3:17); a parable of the low road to the promise and a memorial of judgment on Sodom.
webster_full: ARABAH, the great rift-valley of the Jordan, rendered in the KJV “the plain” and “the champaign.”
It runs from the sea of Chinnereth down to the salt sea (Deu 3:17).
The deepest depression of the earth, the lowest dry land under heaven.
The pilgrim host passed through it toward the promised land (Deu 1:1).
At its floor lies the salt sea, witness to the judgment upon Sodom.
scriptures: Deu 1:1
These be the words which Moses spake unto all Israel on this side Jordan in the wilderness, in the plain over against the Red sea, between Paran, and Tophel, and Laban, and Hazeroth, and Dizahab.
Are they not on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh?
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
corruption_summary: No live redefinition attends this valley; the truth to recover is that the road to the promise runs through the low place, and the salt sea abides as a witness to God’s judgment on sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The Arabah is a plain geographical reality, the Jordan rift and the salt sea basin still measurable as the lowest land on earth.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. The pilgrim way to the inheritance leadeth downward through humbling before it leadeth up to glory, as the believer must be brought low that he may be exalted in due time. And the salt sea remaineth a solemn memorial that God did not spare the cities of the plain, but made them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly. The low road and the dead sea preach humility and holy fear together.
roots_summary: Arabah means a plain, desert, or dry sterile place; it names the Jordan rift and, in the plural, the plains of Moab and of Jericho.
roots_lines: Arabah — Hebrew arabah, a plain, desert, or dry sterile place.
Rendered in the KJV as “the plain,” “the champaign,” and “the desert.”
The plural araboth gives the plains of Moab and the plains of Jericho.
The root conveys aridity and sterility, a waste untilled land.
The sea of the plain is the salt sea, at the valley’s lowest floor.
usage: Moses spake to Israel in the plain, that is, the Arabah, beyond Jordan.
The Arabah runs down to the salt sea, the sea of the plain.
The pilgrim passes through the Arabah, the low road to the promise.

etymology: Hebrew Marah, “bitterness,” from marar, to be bitter; the first camp beyond the Red sea where the waters could not be drunk.
biblical_def: Three days into the wilderness of Shur, the redeemed people who had sung on the far shore of the Red sea found no water; and when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter (Exo 15:23). The song was scarcely ended when the murmuring began. Then Moses cried unto the LORD, and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet; and there He made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there He proved them (Exo 15:25). Marah, the third station beyond the sea (Num 33:8), preacheth the gospel in a figure. Life beyond redemption is not all sweetness; the LORD leadeth His people to bitter waters to prove them and to teach them where the cure lieth. And the cure is a tree cast into the bitterness — a plain type of the cross of Christ, which alone can sweeten the bitter waters of affliction, of conscience, of death itself. Where the tree of Calvary is cast in, the bitter is made sweet. And there the LORD revealed His covenant name: If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God… I am the LORD that healeth thee. Marah is the school where the redeemed learn that their Healer walketh with them, that testing turneth to sweetness, and that the tree maketh every bitter water fit to drink.
webster_summary: The first bitter waters beyond the Red sea, made sweet when the LORD showed Moses a tree to cast in (Exo 15:23-25; Num 33:8); a figure of the cross that heals life’s bitterness, where God revealed Himself the LORD that healeth.
webster_full: MARAH, the bitter waters of the third camp beyond the Red sea (Exo 15:23).
Israel could not drink, for the waters were bitter, and they murmured.
The LORD shewed Moses a tree; cast in, it made the waters sweet.
There He made a statute and proved them, revealing the LORD that healeth.
A figure of the cross that sweetens the bitter waters of affliction.
scriptures: And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah.
Deu 8:16
Who fed thee in the wilderness with manna, which thy fathers knew not, that he might humble thee, and that he might prove thee, to do thee good at thy latter end;
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
corruption_summary: No live redefinition attends Marah; the truth to recover is that God appoints bitter waters to prove His people, and the tree of the cross alone makes them sweet.
corruption_paragraphs: Marah is a real station on the wilderness march, its bitter spring remembered in the record of Israel’s journey.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the redeemed still meet bitter waters, and that God ordaineth them to prove His people and to drive them to the cure. The tree cast into the water is a figure of Christ crucified, by whom the bitterness of affliction and of a guilty conscience is made sweet. And the name revealed at Marah, the LORD that healeth thee, abideth the comfort of the church: her Physician walketh with her through every bitter place.
roots_summary: Marah, from marar, to be bitter; the same root gives Naomi’s cry, Call me Mara, for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.
roots_lines: Marah — Hebrew Marah, “bitterness,” from the root marar, to be bitter.
The same root names the bitter herbs of the passover.
Naomi said, Call me not Naomi, call me Mara (Rth 1:20), of the same stock.
Rapha, to heal, in the covenant name revealed here: the LORD that healeth.
Marah stands opposite Elim, where were twelve wells and threescore and ten palm trees.
usage: They came to Marah and could not drink, for the waters were bitter.
The LORD shewed Moses a tree, and the waters of Marah were made sweet.
At Marah the LORD proved Israel and revealed Himself the LORD that healeth.

etymology: Hebrew Tarah, a station of the wilderness wandering between Tahath and Mithcah; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “station” or “delay.”
biblical_def: Among the two-and-forty stations of Israel’s wandering, recorded by Moses at the LORD’s commandment, standeth the bare name of Tarah: they departed from Tahath, and pitched at Tarah; and they removed from Tarah, and pitched at Mithcah (Num 33:27-28). No event is told of it, no water struck from a rock, no manna, no murmuring, no battle — only that they came, and pitched, and departed. Yet the Holy Ghost was pleased to write down the name. Tarah preacheth the hidden faithfulness of God over the unremembered stages of the pilgrimage. For every camp that Scripture maketh famous, there are many like Tarah, passed over in a line, of which we know nothing but that God brought His people there and led them on. So it is in the believer’s life: a few days shine in memory, marked by great deliverances or great sorrows; but the most are ordinary Tarahs, days of plain travel, of pitching and striking the tent, of which no history will be written. And these too are numbered and ordered by God. He that led Israel by the pillar appointed every removal; not a single stage was left to chance. Let the pilgrim take comfort that the LORD keepeth the record of his obscure days, that his unmarked stages are as truly ordained as his signal mercies, and that the God who wrote down Tarah hath written down every step of the way home.
webster_summary: A bare wilderness station between Tahath and Mithcah in the forty years’ journey (Num 33:27-28); a witness to the hidden faithfulness of God over the unremembered, ordinary stages of the pilgrimage.
webster_full: TARAH, a station of the wilderness wandering between Tahath and Mithcah (Num 33:27).
No event is recorded of it, only that Israel pitched and departed.
Yet the LORD caused its name to be written among the stages.
A witness that God orders the obscure and unremembered days.
The pilgrim’s ordinary stages are numbered as surely as his great mercies.
scriptures: And they journeyed from Rissah, and pitched in Kehelathah.
And they went from Kehelathah, and pitched in mount Shapher.
And they removed from mount Shapher, and encamped in Haradah.
Deu 8:15
Who led thee through that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought, where there was no water; who brought thee forth water out of the rock of flint;
corruption_summary: No live redefinition attends this station; the truth to recover is that God ordains and remembers the obscure, uneventful stages of His people’s pilgrimage.
corruption_paragraphs: Tarah is a real, if obscure, camp on the wilderness itinerary, named in the record of Israel’s journeys.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over the unremarkable. The itinerary of Numbers 33 was written at the LORD’s commandment, and the plain names of camps like Tarah are as much His record as the famous places of miracle. So the believer’s ordinary days, in which nothing is struck from the rock and no enemy falls, are yet ordained and numbered by God. He keepeth the account of every stage of the way home.
roots_summary: The name Tarah is of uncertain meaning, perhaps “station” or “delay”; it appears only in the itinerary of Numbers 33.
roots_lines: Tarah — Hebrew Tarah, a wilderness station of uncertain meaning.
Some connect it with a root for tarrying or delay.
It is not the same name as Terah the father of Abraham, though spelled alike in English.
It lies between Tahath and Mithcah in the list of journeys.
It appears only in Numbers 33, the register of the encampments.
usage: They departed from Tahath, and pitched at Tarah.
Tarah is one of the unremembered stations of the wandering.
Even the bare name of Tarah was written by the LORD’s command.
